title: London, Ont., family raises $500K for daughter's U.S. surgery after being denied funding
summary: A London, Ont., father and daughter who have been fundraising for a major surgery in the United States have now surpassed their goal and are moving ahead with a potentially life-changing procedure…

image.caption: Sydney Gesualdi in 2023, before she was rear-ended at a stop sign leaving her unable to walk. She plans to get surgery in New York early next year. (Submitted by Sydney Gesualdi)

blocks.text: London

A London, Ont., father and daughter who have been fundraising for a major surgery in the United States have now surpassed their goal and are moving ahead with a potentially life-changing procedure that no doctor in Canada would perform.
Sydney Gesualdi is paying out-of-pocket for a surgery she can't get in Canada

After getting rear-ended at a stop sign in 2023, Sydney Gesualdi, now 27, was diagnosed with cranio-cervical instability, a condition involving excessive movement between the skull and the top two vertebrae in the neck, leading to her inability to walk, difficulty breathing, and numbness in her face and limbs.

She was denied spinal consultations by at least eight doctors in Canada, leading the family to consult a neurosurgeon in New York, who recommended cranio-cervical fusion surgery to fuse her skull to her spine—a procedure costing more than $490,000 CAD.
Through a GoFundMe, the family has now raised more than $500,000.
"We're feeling incredibly grateful and a little bit in disbelief," said her father, Joe Gesualdi.

Sydney Gesualdi, now 27, was rear-ended at a red light in July 2023. Since then, she's lost the ability to walk, struggles to breathe and swallow, and experiences extreme fatigue, among other symptoms. (Submitted by Sydney Gesualdi)

Gesualdi started the GoFundMe after the Ontario Ministry of Health denied Sydney's application for full funding through its Out-of-Country Health Services program, leaving the family to raise the money themselves.

London father pushes daughter's wheelchair 200 kilometres to advocate for access to health care

blocks.text: Even after reaching the fundraising goal, people have continued to send in donations, he said, adding that donors are sending money in case the cost changes, or to cover other costs while in the U.S.
Gesualdi said the family is currently in touch with Mount Sinai Hospital in New York and looking at a date in early 2027.
Once the date is finalized, the family will be posting the journey on social media to document it and "show the public where their gifts have gone," he said.
Advocating for change
Along with the fundraising effort, Gesualdi has been working to raise awareness of Sydney's struggle to access treatment in Ontario.

In August, he set out on a six-week, 200-kilometre journey to push her empty wheelchair on foot from London to Queen's Park, stopping along the way to hand out flyers and tell Sydney's story to people he met.
He hoped the walk would also capture the attention of Premier Doug Ford, the Ministry of Health and other decision-makers.
Earlier this week, he and Sydney also met with Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

While they were grateful for the opportunity, he said he expected the ministry would review the out-of-country funding application. He also hoped to discuss their experience in order to improve accessibility to the program.

"We were disappointed to essentially enter the meeting and restate everything that is on the public record to them," Gesualdi said. "Instead of talking about fixes and experiences with the system, we had the system and the way that it works reflected back to us."
"We did request an additional meeting, but there was no commitment to do that."

Joe Gesualdi (left) handing out flyers on his walk to Queen's Park, sharing the details about his daughter Sydney Gesualdi's story and advocating for more accessible out-of-country healthcare treatment. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)
The Ministry of Health said in a statement on Friday that in order to get out-of-country funding approved, a physician must submit a request on behalf of the patient.
"Physicians are responsible for the coordination of health care for their patients," wrote Lily Barnes, the ministry's spokesperson.

"This includes determining the urgency of their patients' need for health services and referrals to other appropriate health care providers and facilities, including referrals outside of province or country."
But that would have required a consultation with a Canadian surgeon, which Sydney could not get.
Gesualdi is now calling for a review of the out-of-country funding program to make it more accessible to other Ontarians dealing with issues like his daughter's.
He believes the process has become too bureaucratic, administered by "career officials" rather than physicians, and that, ultimately, the ministry makes the final decisions itself.
In his view, there are also "a lot of medical assumptions being made in the process," he said, and too few professional opinions being considered.
"The results speak for themselves," he said. "It's continuous denial after denial."
